data.title: Gap expands AI shopping with Alta Daily and new discovery tools
data.description:
Gap Inc. is pushing artificial intelligence (AI) deeper into how its shoppers discover and style its products.

The retailer on Monday unveiled new natural-language product discovery features for its Old Navy and Banana Republic brands. Separately, Gap said it’s launching an online styling experience with Alta Daily. The feature brings Gap’s namesake-brand merchandise into AI-generated outfit recommendations on the third-party styling app.

The announcements coincide with the retailer’s 30th anniversary of launching Gap Online in 1996. The company has been highlighting that milestone during this week’s SF Tech Week in San Francisco, framing AI as the next evolution in how customers shop its brands. Gap said it is also exploring emerging agentic commerce, in which AI can take actions on a shopper’s behalf.

“Thirty years ago, we launched gap.com, revolutionizing the way customers interacted with our brands, and today AI is creating a new opportunity to rethink how people shop for fashion,” Gap chief technology officer Sven Gerjets said in a statement.

Gap Inc., which owns Gap, Banana Republic, Old Navy and Athleta, ranks No. 20 in the Top 2000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales and more.

Gap adds AI styling through Alta Daily

Rather than relying only on search boxes and product grids, Gap said it is experimenting with AI tools that can “increasingly understand intent, context and individual preferences.”

As part of that push, Gap is bringing its products into Alta Daily, the AI-powered digital closet and personal styling app. Shoppers can incorporate Gap-brand merchandise into personalized outfit recommendations and visualize the looks on their Alta avatars. The experience “brings AI-powered styling and discovery into a more visual and personalized environment,” Gap said.

To build their virtual wardrobes, Alta users can also digitize clothes they already own. From there, Alta says its app can generate outfits based on factors such as the user’s existing closet, personal style, schedule and weather.

That approach overlaps with the agentic-commerce model Gap says it has been exploring. Alta founder and CEO Jenny Wang told TechCrunch earlier this year that agentic commerce needs “a data layer that understands the shopper’s style preferences.” That data can include a shopper’s closet, past purchases and avatar, she said.

Meanwhile, shoppers can also find Gap Inc. products through Daydream, an AI-powered fashion platform that lets shoppers describe what they want in everyday language. Gap was already directing shoppers to the daydream.ing platform as a product-discovery option during the 2025 holiday season.

Old Navy and Banana Republic add AI tools

Gap is also reworking product discovery at Old Navy and Banana Republic around conversational AI. The tools let shoppers describe what they want in natural language and receive product ideas and recommendations.

Rather than translating an idea into keywords or filters, Gap said the AI tools are designed “to better understand customer intent and help people move more naturally from an idea to products that fit what they had in mind.”

Gap did not specify whether they are available through the brands’ websites, mobile apps or both.

Gap builds out AI strategy

The launches are part of a broader AI strategy Gap has been building across its ecommerce business. In 2024, the retailer established a dedicated Office of AI, focusing on “early use cases, primarily related to employee enablement,” Richard Dickson, Gap’s president and CEO, said at the time. Since then, the retailer has rolled out AI tools in customer service, personalized recommendations, fulfillment and other areas.

Gap is also directing some of its increased capital spending toward that work. During the company’s August earnings call, chief financial officer Katrina O’Connell said Gap’s capital expenditures will reach $650 million in fiscal 2026, up from $470 million last year. Some of those funds will flow into “the technology work that we’re doing around AI to be able to build capability,” she said.

Agentic commerce is a newer area for the company. In March, Gap became a launch partner for Bold Metrics’ Agent Sizing Protocol. By asking shoppers about fit and preferences, the technology helps conversational shopping agents determine the right apparel size.

At the same time, Gap announced support for Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol. The open standard, co-developed with Shopify, connects merchants with AI-powered shopping and checkout experiences. With the protocol, shoppers will be able to find and purchase Gap products using AI Mode in Google Search and in the Gemini app.

Gap was already bringing AI into the customer experience last year. Ahead of the 2025 holiday season, the retailer rolled out personalized recommendations and a digital assistant through the “Chat with Us” feature on its brands’ ecommerce sites and mobile apps.

Underlying many of those efforts is Gap’s partnership with Google Cloud. Launched in 2025, the partnership gives Gap access to Google technologies, including Gemini, Vertex AI and BigQuery.

data.title: Ikea, Kodiak prepare to launch driverless freight service in Texas
data.description:
After four years of testing autonomous freight with a safety driver behind the wheel, Ikea is preparing to go fully driverless in Texas using Kodiak’s autonomous driving technology.

Later this year, the Sweden-based home furnishings retailer plans to launch driverless service with Kodiak on a roughly 220-mile stretch connecting the Houston and Dallas metro areas. The highway leg is part of a nearly 300-mile delivery route moving Ikea goods from its Baytown distribution center to its store in Frisco.

“IKEA has been a wonderful partner and customer for four years, and this represents the next chapter,” Don Burnette, Kodiak’s founder and CEO, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Sept. 29.

Originally intended as a three-month trial, the pilot between Ikea and Kodiak continued for four years. During that span, Kodiak said its trucks carried more than 1,300 Ikea loads and logged more than 750,000 autonomous miles. The company described the service as operating “without incident” and with a “nearly perfect” on-time delivery record.

The launch comes as autonomous freight moves beyond small-scale pilots and into day-to-day operations. Walmart, Kroger and Loblaw have all tested or deployed autonomous vehicles for middle-mile deliveries, while PepsiCo said it’s expanding driverless freight across several states.

Ikea ranks No. 6 in the Europe Database, Digital Commerce 360’s ranking of the largest online retailers in the region by their annual ecommerce sales. There, Digital Commerce 360 categorizes it as a Housewares & Home Furnishings retailer.

How Kodiak is preparing for driverless freight

In a Sept. 29 update, Kodiak said it has hauled Ikea goods along the Texas route day and night, seven days a week, and through varying weather conditions. Later this year, Ikea will become Kodiak’s launch shipper for driverless long-haul highway service, with no safety driver aboard.

Kodiak provides the autonomous driving system behind the trucks. Its core product, the Kodiak Driver, combines AI-powered software with modular hardware installed on commercial vehicles. The company offers the technology through a Driver-as-a-Service model and strategic partnerships.

Before it removes safety drivers, Kodiak is also completing its final round of testing. In a Sept. 25 release, the company shared that its trucks have been making deliveries between its Lancaster, Texas, hub and Houston since August without the driver taking control, including on surface streets. Kodiak said it’s also running closed-course tests to recreate situations “that occur too rarely, or are too risky, to test on public highways.”

“Our progress since beginning our final push towards driverless commercial deliveries has been incredible, and it is a strong signal we are ready to scale unsupervised driverless service on long-haul lanes,” Burnette said in the Sept. 25 release.

Kodiak already operates without drivers in another setting. Since December 2024, Atlas Energy Solutions has used customer-owned trucks equipped with the Kodiak Driver to haul freight in the Permian Basin of West Texas and eastern New Mexico. As of June, Kodiak reported that 35 Atlas trucks using the system had logged more than 40,000 hours of paid driverless operations.

What driverless freight could mean for Ikea

With Ikea, Kodiak is taking that technology from an industrial setting to a major interstate freight lane. The company said four years of testing also taught it how to integrate autonomous trucks into Ikea’s supply chain, from scheduling departures and unloading docks to using vehicle data for predictive maintenance.

“We now know exactly what it takes to transform the underlying technology into an AI-driven product that generates value and efficiency,” Kodiak said in its Sept. 29 blog post.

Ikea has already seen some of those potential benefits elsewhere. After testing, Ikea China permanently adopted self-driving electric vehicles at its Hefei operation, Ingka Group said in March. Ingka is Ikea’s largest franchisee and operates its U.S. retail business, including 61 retail locations.

The vehicles move goods between a warehouse and the store for customer pickup orders and restocking. During the test, the trucks traveled nearly 75,600 kilometers, or about 47,000 miles, according to Ingka. The company said they cut average wait times for pickup orders from six hours to two. Transportation costs between Ikea locations also fell by more than 50%.

Ikea is also testing autonomous deliveries directly to customers in China. Ingka said it is evaluating whether the Hefei model could work in other markets where regulations and infrastructure allow.

Other companies expand driverless freight

Retailers and consumer brands are increasingly using autonomous trucks for middle-mile routes.

Walmart was an early adopter. In 2021, the retailer and autonomous trucking company Gatik removed the safety driver from box trucks running a roughly 7-mile route between a Walmart facility and a neighborhood market in Bentonville, Arkansas. According to Gatik, it was “the first time an autonomous trucking company has removed the safety driver from a commercial delivery route on the middle mile.”

More recently, in June, PepsiCo signed a multiyear agreement with Gatik to expand autonomous freight across its North American supply chain. Driverless trucks are already operating for PepsiCo in Texas, Arizona and Arkansas. FreightWaves reported that the network serves about 250 retail locations, including Walmart and Dollar General stores. Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales. Dollar General is ranked No. 674 in the Top 1000.

Meanwhile, the economics of autonomous trucking may depend heavily on distance and scale. A 2026 study by researchers at North Dakota State University estimated potential savings of about 13% for a 200-mile hub-to-hub route, rising to 31% at 1,000 miles when fleets reach sufficient scale.

Without that scale, shorter autonomous routes could cost more, they found. The study did not examine Ikea, but its roughly 220-mile driverless leg is close to the shorter route modeled.

data.title: How Angara prepares for the Cyber 5, shifting consumer behavior
data.description:
Online-only jewelry retailer Angara has been preparing for the Cyber 5 by increasing its focus on flexibility, according to co-founder and CEO Ankur Daga.

That means giving its customers more choices and using data to respond faster to consumer behaviors. It also means “removing friction between inspiration and purchase,” Daga told Digital Commerce 360.

The Cyber 5 refers to the five-day period of Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday. And in 2025, the holiday shopping season taught Angara that “the companies that can listen and adapt in real time have a very different advantage from those trying to predict the customer months ahead,” he explained.

Among the retailer’s biggest lessons from 2025’s peak season was learning just how quickly consumer preferences can change in such periods, he said. In the jewelry space, a traditional retailer could be making inventory decisions for the holidays about five or six months in advance. But by the time retailers know what consumers want, it can be too late to react, he added.

“For us, that reinforced the importance of staying as close to real-time demand as possible,” Daga said. “Because we manufacture just in time, we’re not sitting on large amounts of finished inventory. We can see what customers are responding to — whether that’s a particular gemstone, shape, metal or price point — and adjust very quickly.”

Angara is No. 363 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Angara is also No. 192 in Digital Commerce 360’s new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Angara’s approach leading up to the Cyber 5

Daga said Angara’s busiest periods are the holiday season and Valentine’s Day. Both also overlap with a “major engagement season.”

“From a business standpoint, our model is built to respond to demand in real time rather than forecasting it months in advance,” Daga said. “Because we own our entire supply chain, we’re able to adjust and produce as we see what customers are actually buying. During peak periods, preparation is as much about manufacturing capacity, technology and redundancy as it is about inventory.”

Daga said the Cyber 5 is an opportunity for Angara to ensure its ecommerce and manufacturing systems “can flex with demand.” The retailer’s holiday data indicates that its customers behave differently during the period.

The share of lab-grown gemstone sales increases, as does the share of stones above one carat. Stone shapes like the oval and emerald cut become more prominent.

“At the same time, the broader consumer environment is increasingly K-shaped, so we need to be prepared for shoppers trading up as well as those looking for greater value,” Daga said. “That means having the right mix of gemstones and diamonds available across sizes and qualities, sufficient manufacturing capacity and redundancy, and an ecommerce experience that makes it easy for customers to understand their options.”

He said Angara’s just-in-time model “is particularly valuable during the Cyber 5” because the retailer can watch demand develop and then adapt production around what customers are choosing.

How Angara improves its KPIs

Daga said Angara’s most effective strategy for improving its conversion rate and average order value (AOV) has been giving its customers more choices. At the same time, though, it has to make those choices easier to navigate.

“Jewelry is an incredibly personal purchase, so rather than pushing everyone toward a single product or price point, we allow customers to customize across metals, gemstones, stone quality and natural or lab-grown options,” Daga said. “That creates various options around a design and lets a customer trade up — or down — based on what matters most to them.”

Angara is also investing in richer product-page content and education. Daga explained that that’s because jewelry customers tend to do “a great deal” of research before completing their purchases.

Partially as a result of those refinements, Angara has seen a 500% year-over-year increase in traffic from its top three artificial intelligence (AI) referral sources, according to Daga.

“What we try not to do is optimize conversion simply by reducing quality or taking material out of a piece to reach an arbitrary price point,” Daga said. “Particularly with fine jewelry, there is a point at which making something lighter or thinner changes how it feels and wears.”

He noted that Angara would prefer to create value for consumers through aspects such as gemstone size, material or customization rather than compromise on a product’s quality.

data.title: Levi's reports 10% ecommerce growth, eyes stronger holiday sales
data.description:
Levi Strauss & Co. reported a 10% increase in ecommerce revenue in its fiscal third quarter, outpacing growth across its broader direct-to-consumer (DTC) business.

DTC revenue, which includes sales through the company’s own stores and ecommerce channels, rose 2% year over year in the retailer’s third quarter ended Aug. 30. Weakness in the U.S. and Europe weighed on results, although stronger wholesale sales helped lift overall revenue. In Q3, total company revenue increased 4% to $1.61 billion, up from $1.54 billion a year earlier.

“We saw strong growth in our international and wholesale businesses, and continued momentum across our lifestyle categories,” said Michelle Gass, president and CEO of Levi Strauss & Co., in the company’s earnings release. “While our direct-to-consumer business fell short of our internal expectations, we moved quickly to address the shortfall and are encouraged by the strength we are seeing heading into the holiday season, including in the U.S.”

Levi Strauss is No. 148 in the Top 2000 Database. The market research tool ranks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales and more.

Levi Strauss web sales by year

 

Levi’s expands ecommerce with AI shopping assistant

After another quarter of double-digit ecommerce growth, Levi Strauss is stepping up investments in its online shopping experience, including the launch of an AI shopping assistant in the U.S.

The tool provides styling advice and helps shoppers “discover new styles and build complete outfits,” Gass told analysts on the company’s Q3 earnings call Wednesday (Oct. 7).

Early results are encouraging. Shoppers who use the assistant add products to their bags at roughly three times the average rate, according to Gass.

The company has also upgraded Levi.com with “richer storytelling, more dynamic videos and inspirational styling content,” she said.

More changes are on the way. Levi Strauss is preparing a broader redesign and platform migration of Levi.com, both slated for a global launch in 2027, she said. The updated site will offer more personalized shopping experiences, outfit recommendations and what Gass described as “immersive fit navigation.” One goal, she said, is to “convert more consumers into head-to-toe lifestyle shoppers.”

Levi’s responds to slower DTC growth

Despite ecommerce gains, Levi’s broader DTC business faced challenges during the quarter.

In Q3, DTC revenue increased 8% in Asia and 2% in the Americas. Within the Americas, U.S. DTC revenue fell 1%, while Europe recorded a 2% decline. Global DTC comparable sales were flat.

Wholesale, meanwhile, grew 6%. The results underscored the importance of the company’s “DTC first but not DTC-only” strategy, as Gass described it.

In Europe, unusually warm weather kept shoppers away for much of the quarter, she said. In the U.S., Levi’s back-to-school campaign failed to generate the traffic and demand the company expected. The campaign emphasized loose-fitting denim just as consumer interest was shifting toward low-rise styles, Gass explained.

Levi’s responded by redirecting its marketing toward low-rise fits and other “areas of strong consumer demand.” Gass said it also refreshed its marketing campaign and store merchandising, stepped up digital and social media efforts, and worked to strengthen inventory positions in popular styles.

Those efforts are beginning to pay off. U.S. DTC returned to growth in September, while European trends improved as temperatures cooled. Gass said global DTC was tracking at a mid-single-digit growth rate early in Q4. For the full fiscal year, Levi’s projects high-single-digit DTC growth.

Levi’s expansion beyond denim

Levi Strauss is also making progress toward becoming what it calls a “head-to-toe” lifestyle brand.

In Q3, categories outside Levi’s core denim bottoms business accounted for roughly half of the company’s revenue growth, Gass said. Tops were a notable contributor, with sales up 7% overall and 10% in women’s tops.

The shift toward higher-end apparel is also gaining momentum. Levi’s premium Blue Tab collection delivered “strong double-digit growth” across men’s and women’s apparel, according to Gass.

Featuring Japanese selvedge denim, the line is expanding into elevated products such as cashmere, silk and tailored pieces, she said, with price points ranging from $200 to $500.

Gass also sees room to grow. Levi’s holds less than 1% of the super-premium jeans market, Gass said, despite the brand’s broader leadership in denim.

“And that should at least be commensurate with our market share overall,” she said.

Levi’s reinvests tariff refunds ahead of holiday shopping season

As it heads into the holiday shopping season, Levi Strauss is putting much of an approximately $80 million tariff refund benefit back into its business.

The company plans to reinvest roughly three-quarters of the benefit, or about $60 million, across Q3 and Q4. Those funds will support additional marketing, supply chain improvements and what Gass called “sharper value for consumers during key holiday promotional moments.”

Levi’s is also preparing what Gass described as its “most robust activation plan in years.” Holiday initiatives include experiential pop-ups, improved in-store experiences, personalized styling and curated gift assortments.

“Combined with strong product newness and focused commercial execution, these efforts are designed to drive traffic, improve conversion and deepen consumer connection with the Levi’s brand,” Gass said.

data.title: Albertsons expands OpenAI work, adding enterprise ChatGPT use
data.description:
Albertsons Companies continues to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) best fits into its operations and ecommerce strategy, which now includes an expanded enterprise partnership with OpenAI and a ChatGPT plugin for the Safeway banner.

OpenAI detailed the companies’ latest work in a blog post on Oct. 1, noting that Albertsons’ teams were using ChatGPT to “navigate complexity, accelerate workflows and move promising ideas toward production faster.”

Albertsons is No. 17 in the Top 1000 Database. That database ranks the largest online retailers in North America by annual ecommerce sales.

OpenAI described the scope of its work with Albertsons as including ChatGPT Enterprise, in addition to what it referred to as “custom AI-powered experiences for its customers, data-driven recommendations and promotional insights built with the OpenAI API.”

Albertsons’ portfolio included more than 2,200 stores across its banners. Those banners encompass its namesake stores, Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Shaw’s, ACME and Tom Thumb.

Albertsons rolled out its Safeway plugin for ChatGPT in August.

“Research tells us that consumers are increasingly interested in using AI to help with grocery shopping,” said Jill Pavlovich, senior vice president, digital customer experience at Albertsons Companies, at the time. “By enabling our plugin in ChatGPT, we are making grocery shopping as simple as having a conversation by meeting our customers when and how they choose to shop.”

The plugin operates within the ChatGPT app experience. Once connected to ChatGPT and a shopper’s Safeway account, it enables a chat-style interface for planning grocery lists and making purchases.

Albertsons’ recent history of AI use

Previously, Albertsons became one of the first retailers to test ChatGPT’s ads in 2026. OpenAI welcomed the grocer, along with Target and Williams-Sonoma in the pilot, and its ads have continued to evolve alongside ChatGPT’s agentic commerce strategy throughout the year.

In addition to OpenAI, Albertsons has also worked with Google on an AI assistant experience. Notably, Albertsons was the first retailer to use Google Cloud’s conversational AI solution in 2025.

Looking ahead, OpenAI expects Albertsons to leverage its large language model to create internal predictive models, along with recommendations and insights about the grocer’s activities, thanks to employee tools, commerce-related apps and advertising solutions that OpenAI will power there.
